A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same convolutional Fenchel–Young loss framework. Their main texts, equations, proofs, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable, and retained material can be matched despite reformatting and appendix reorganization.

before.justification: v1 contains theoretical results, algorithms, illustrative task formulations, and proofs, but no original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

after.justification: Appendix F reports original ImageNet-1k classification experiments and CIFAR-10/100 classification and rejection experiments, including accuracy, acceptance rates, and measured runtime.

M1.justification: The general loss construction, prediction link, and multiclass Algorithm 1 are retained. Appendix D adds concrete procedural extensions: a rejection-specific loss with a closed-form O(K) minimizer, and a Precision@k loss with the new capped-simplex solver in Algorithm 2. These substantially expand the implemented mathematical procedures.

E1.justification: v1 has no dataset experiments. Appendix F adds ImageNet-1k multiclass classification and CIFAR-10/100 ordinary classification and classification with rejection. The new Precision@k and binary examples are analytical rather than additional dataset evaluations.

E2.justification: v3 introduces a limited comparison set: standard cross-entropy in the ImageNet experiment, and the authors' ordinary-classification loss as a reference for rejection on CIFAR. Figure 1 additionally compares analytical loss and probability-estimation curves against logistic loss and sigmoid. These reported comparisons are absent from v1.

E3.justification: Appendix F introduces entirely new evaluation protocols: ResNet-50 on ImageNet with 120-epoch training, and WideResNet-28 on CIFAR with specified optimization and augmentation settings. Rejection uses cost 0.05, system accuracy defined through the 0-1-c loss, and acceptance rate. These are new protocols, not revisions of existing experiments.

E4.justification: Appendix E adds a focused binary case study comparing loss geometry and probability estimators, showing the linear loss region and probability plateau in Figure 1. Appendix F also measures computational overhead through epoch runtimes. Neither version provides component ablations or systematic robustness sweeps.

E5.justification: v3 first reports averages over three independent ImageNet runs and five CIFAR runs, and invokes a t-test at the 5% level for the ImageNet comparison. Reporting remains limited: the tables contain no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or exact p-values. v1 has no empirical statistical reporting.

E6.justification: All empirical results are new. Table 1 reports ImageNet accuracy of 76.81% versus 76.40% for cross-entropy, with 653.63 versus 647.22 seconds per epoch. Table 2 reports CIFAR-10/100 rejection system accuracies of 96.79%/91.90% and acceptance rates of 92.84%/65.94%, alongside ordinary-classification accuracies of 93.87%/74.36%. System accuracy and ordinary accuracy are different metrics, not directly comparable performance gains.

T1.justification: The original central theorems and proofs are retained or relocated. New material includes rejection and Precision@k solver derivations, the rejection regret constant of 2, explicit binary formulas, and Theorem 25's quantitative probability-estimation bound. However, the new Precision@k derivation inconsistently drops the 1/k scaling between equation (37) and equation (39)/Algorithm 2.

C1.justification: The central claims remain the constructive existence of convex smooth surrogates with linear regret bounds for arbitrary discrete losses, improved regret constants, and consistent probability estimation. The new conclusion and additional task examples support this already-stated scope rather than establish a broader central claim.

C2.justification: Appendix A substantially expands the interpretation of statistical advantages, distinguishing parametric and nonparametric rates, rejecting universal superiority, and discussing benefits of nonconvex alternatives. Appendix E explains the linear region near decision boundaries. Appendix F adds interpretations of practical optimization compatibility, rejection behavior, and runtime. The earlier strong-convexity discussion is largely relocated.

D1.justification: v3 adds substantial reproducibility information absent from v1: experimental architectures, optimizer parameters, learning-rate schedules, batch sizes, training duration, eight RTX 3090 GPUs, CIFAR augmentation and normalization procedures, and measured epoch runtimes. These document newly introduced experiments rather than reveal changes to an earlier experimental setup.

R1.justification: v3 substantially expands research positioning through information geometry and Bregman-divergence connections, comparisons with fast-rate and nonconvex losses, and additional rejection literature. Appendix G explicitly relates its probability-estimation bound to generalized Fenchel–Young losses. These are substantive additions beyond reference renumbering and publication-metadata updates.

P1.justification: The core section sequence and much of the original prose remain. v3 makes local wording and notation edits, adds a conclusion, moves the proofs of Theorem 13 and Corollary 16 into the appendix, and relocates the strong-convexity discussion. Most expansion comes from new substantive content rather than wholesale rewriting.

P2.justification: v3 adopts the NeurIPS layout, changing the title block, typography, text width, and equation placement throughout. It also adds the two-panel Figure 1, two empirical tables, and Algorithm 2. v1 contains no figures or experimental tables, so the visual presentation changes substantially beyond pagination.

improvement.justification: The first empirical comparisons, detailed training recipes, and more qualified discussion improve the practical support and assessability of the retained central theory. The net gain is limited by narrow comparisons and sparse uncertainty reporting, together with the new Precision@k scaling inconsistency in equation (37), equation (39), and Algorithm 2. That correctness issue weakens one added procedural extension without changing the retained main construction.
